title: The sodium gate opens
q: For a typical neuron near its resting potential, voltage-gated sodium channels open. In which direction is the initial net sodium movement?
why: Under these usual conditions, sodium enters through open sodium channels down its electrochemical gradient. Other currents can also affect the membrane.

title: The potassium gate opens
q: During the falling phase of a typical neuronal action potential, voltage-gated potassium channels open. In which direction is the net potassium movement?
why: During the usual falling phase, potassium leaves the neuron through open potassium channels, helping bring the membrane potential back down.

title: A positive current crosses
q: In a simplified neuron model, positive sodium charge enters and other currents are neglected. What happens initially to the inside voltage relative to outside?
why: Net inward positive charge makes the inside less negative relative to the outside: a depolarization in this simplified case.

title: A positive current leaves
q: In a simplified neuron model, positive potassium charge leaves and other currents are neglected. What happens initially to the inside voltage relative to outside?
why: Net outward positive charge makes the inside more negative relative to the outside, contributing to repolarization during a typical action potential.

title: A signal reaches a terminal
q: At a typical chemical synapse, an arriving action potential opens presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels. Where does calcium initially move?
options: Out of the terminal into the cleft
why: Calcium enters the presynaptic terminal through voltage-gated channels. Its entry initiates a cascade that helps synaptic vesicles fuse with the membrane.

title: Calcium changes the terminal
q: At a typical chemical synapse, calcium enters the presynaptic terminal. What event does it help trigger?
options: Synaptic vesicles fuse with the membrane
The axon becomes a blood vessel
why: Calcium entry helps trigger synaptic vesicle fusion with the presynaptic membrane, allowing neurotransmitter release.

title: A vesicle opens to the gap
q: When a neurotransmitter-containing vesicle fuses with the presynaptic membrane, where is its soluble neurotransmitter released?
why: Vesicle fusion releases neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft, the extracellular gap between the cells.

title: The message finds a receptor
q: After release at a chemical synapse, what can a neurotransmitter bind on the receiving cell?
why: Neurotransmitter can cross the cleft and bind a compatible postsynaptic receptor. The resulting response depends on the receptor and cell.

title: Clearing the signal
q: At a synapse where neurotransmitter is removed by presynaptic reuptake, where does that transporter return it?
why: Presynaptic reuptake returns some neurotransmitter from the cleft into the sending neuron. Diffusion and enzymatic breakdown are other possible clearance mechanisms.
